readerTitle: The $3,000 edge that's worth less than the $800 one
caseNote: 가상 사례 (비스트로, 미용실 예약 앱) + 실제 연구 (Mueller의 장기 수익률 연구, McGrath의 일시적 우위론) · 사례 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 우위의 가치는 오늘의 크기가 아니라 '크기 × 경쟁자가 따라잡기까지 걸리는 시간'으로 잰다.
misconception: 지금 더 큰 이익을 주는 우위가 더 좋은 우위다. 한번 앞서면 계속 앞선다.

sources.text: Mueller, D. C. (1986). Profits in the Long Run. Cambridge University Press.
McGrath, R. G. (2013). The End of Competitive Advantage. Harvard Business Review Press.
비스트로·예약 앱 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 예약 앱 계산: AI 기능 $10,000 × 3개월 = $30,000. 결제 단말 연동 $3,000 × 최소 24개월 = $72,000 이상. 설치·유지 비용은 두 안이 같다고 단순화했습니다.
Mueller(1986)는 미국 기업의 초과 이익이 시간이 지나며 평균으로 수렴하지만 일부 기업은 장기간 평균 이상을 유지한다는 결과를 보고했습니다. 카드에는 수치 없이 일반적 경향으로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 요약 표현을 원문과 대조하세요.
McGrath(2013)의 주장(빠르게 변하는 시장에서는 일시적 우위를 연속으로 이어가는 것이 중요하다)을 요약했습니다. 표현이 원문 취지와 맞는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The $3,000 edge that's worth less than the $800 one
body: A restaurant owner has money for one bet this year. A new signature dish would add about $3,000 a month in profit. A five-year lease on the only terrace on the street would add about $800.
The first number is almost four times bigger. It is still the smaller prize.

image.label: A plated dish and a sunny terrace on two sides of a scale
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 저울 왼쪽에 화려한 대표 요리 접시("$3,000/mo" 태그), 오른쪽에 작은 테라스 테이블("$800/mo" 태그). 저울이 의외로 테라스 쪽으로 기울어 있음. 실제 식당 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Dish or terrace?
body: You run a busy bistro. The signature dish adds $3,000 a month, but the restaurants next door could copy it within about four months.
The terrace lease adds $800 a month, and no one else on the street can get a terrace for five years. Both cost about the same to set up. Which is worth more?

options.text: The dish. It earns almost four times more each month
options.feedback: You win the first few months, but once neighbors copy it the extra profit fades. Four months of $3,000 is about $12,000 in total.

options.text: The terrace. It earns less, but nobody can match it
options.feedback: $800 a month for 60 months is $48,000, four times the dish. You give up fast cash for an edge that keeps paying.

options.text: The dish, because quick profit can fund the next bet
options.feedback: Fast cash has real value, and chaining bets is smart. But in total it's $12,000 against $48,000, so it only makes sense if you can still get the terrace too.

cards.title: The dish wins for 15 months. Then it stops.
body: Assume the dish's extra profit drops to zero once rivals copy it. The terrace earns steadily until the lease ends. Here is the total extra profit from each.
cards.callout: Value of an edge = **extra profit per month × months it lasts**.

cards.title: Sustainable advantage
body: A **sustainable advantage** is an edge that keeps paying after rivals have seen it and tried to copy it.
The test isn't how big the edge is today. It's how long it survives competition. A bigger edge that disappears in a season can be worth far less than a modest one that holds for years.

image.label: Two profit lines: a tall spike that drops and a low line that keeps going
image.brief: 그래프 인포그래픽. 가로축은 시간. 빨간 선은 높게 치솟았다가 경쟁자 아이콘이 등장하는 지점에서 0으로 떨어짐("Copied"). 초록 선은 낮지만 오른쪽 끝까지 평평하게 이어짐. 두 선 아래 면적을 칠해 초록 면적이 더 크게 보이도록.

cards.title: Most extra profit fades. Not all of it.
body: Economists who track company profits over many years see a common pattern. Firms earning well above average tend to drift back toward average as rivals enter, copy and undercut. Dennis Mueller's long-run studies of US companies are a well-known example.
But the drift is not complete. Some firms stay above average for a long time. What sets them apart is usually not a bigger first edge. It's an edge that rivals find **slow or hard to match**.

cards.title: Ask one question: how long to copy?
body: Before you invest in an edge, estimate how long a determined rival would need to match it.
list: **Weeks:** a price cut, a promotion, a new menu item
**Months:** a new feature, a new service, a redesign
**Years:** a scarce location, a trusted reputation, long supplier relationships, a well-trained team
cards.callout: Why some edges are so hard to copy is the next lesson.

cards.title: Nothing lasts forever, and time is a guess.
body: Leases end, tastes shift, and new technology can make a durable edge irrelevant. Your estimate of "months to copy" is a judgment, not a fact.

Short edges aren't worthless either. Rita McGrath argues in *The End of Competitive Advantage* that in fast-moving markets, firms win by chaining many temporary advantages. Take quick wins, but don't build your whole plan on them lasting. And a lasting edge can make owners comfortable just when they should keep improving.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app for salons.
body: Your team can build one thing this quarter. An AI scheduling assistant would add about $10,000 a month in profit, but rivals could ship something similar in about three months.
Direct links with the three payment terminals most salons already use would add $3,000 a month. They need partner deals, so rivals would need two years or more.

options.text: Build the AI assistant first. It's the bigger win
options.feedback: A real win of about $30,000 before rivals catch up. Worth doing later, but not instead of the edge that lasts.
$3,000 a month for at least 24 months is $72,000 or more. Slower to show, but rivals can't erase it next quarter.

options.text: Skip both and cut prices 30% to win users
options.feedback: Rivals can match a price cut in a day. You'd give up margin for an edge that may last only until they notice.

cards.title: Value an edge by how long it lasts, not how big it looks.
body: An advantage is worth its size multiplied by the time before rivals close the gap.
**Try it today:** list your three biggest advantages. Next to each, write how many months a determined rival would need to copy it.
